questions.q: Global malabsorption means defective absorption of:
questions.exp: Global malabsorption: defective absorption of a. carbohydrate, b. fat, c. protein. (Book p18)

questions.q: Among the nutrients in global malabsorption, fat is described as:
opts: Most sensitive & specific, and the most energy dense nutrient
Only a marker of pancreatic disease
questions.exp: b. Fat: most sensitive & specific, most energy dense nutrient. (Book p18)

questions.q: Global malabsorption results from:
questions.exp: Global malabsorption: small intestinal mucosal dysfunction. (Book p18)

questions.q: The three causes of global malabsorption listed are:
opts: Celiac disease, Whipple's disease and tropical sprue
Cystinuria, Hartnup disease and enterokinase deficiency
questions.exp: Causes: a. celiac disease, b. Whipple's disease, c. tropical sprue. (Book p18)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not a listed cause of global malabsorption:
questions.exp: Global malabsorption causes: celiac disease, Whipple's disease, tropical sprue. Chronic pancreatitis is a luminal defect. (Book p18)

questions.q: Celiac disease is also known as:
opts: Celiac sprue / gluten sensitive enteropathy / non-tropical sprue
questions.exp: Features: AKA celiac sprue / gluten sensitive enteropathy / non-tropical sprue. (Book p18)

questions.q: In the iceberg phenomenon, what proportion present with classical features?
questions.exp: Iceberg phenomenon: only 50% present with classical features. (Book p18)

questions.q: The iceberg phenomenon is attributed to:
opts: Physician unawareness, so cases are missed
A very low prevalence of the disease
questions.exp: Iceberg phenomenon: only 50% present with classical features; due to physician unawareness — diagnosis missed. (Book p18)

questions.q: The most important predisposition to celiac disease is:
questions.exp: HLA DQ2 / DQ8: most important predisposition. (Book p18)

questions.q: Celiac disease is described as a ____ small intestinal disease.
questions.exp: Celiac disease is a proximal small intestinal disease. (Book p18)

questions.q: In the celiac iceberg image, EMA stands for ____ antibody.
questions.exp: Image key: EMA — endomysial antibody; Ig — immunoglobulin; tTG — tissue transglutaminase. (Book p18)

questions.q: In the celiac iceberg image, tTG stands for tissue ____.
questions.exp: Image key: tTG — tissue transglutaminase. (Book p18)

questions.q: Match the celiac type to the printed definition — 1) Classical 2) Atypical 3) Silent 4) Latent … A) Asymptomatic, serology positive B) 50% of cases present with symptoms of malabsorption C) Asymptomatic, antibodies negative D) Presents with symptoms other than malabsorption
questions.exp: Classical: 50% of cases present with symptoms of malabsorption; atypical: symptoms other than malabsorption; silent: asymptomatic with positive serology; latent: asymptomatic with negative antibodies. (Book p18)

questions.q: Classical celiac disease is defined as:
opts: 50% of cases presenting with symptoms of malabsorption
questions.exp: Classical celiac disease: 50% of cases present with symptoms of malabsorption. (Book p18)

questions.q: Atypical celiac disease presents with:
questions.exp: Atypical celiac disease: presents with symptoms other than malabsorption. (Book p18)

questions.q: Silent celiac disease is:
questions.exp: Silent celiac disease: asymptomatic, serology positive. (Book p18)

questions.q: Latent celiac disease is:
opts: Asymptomatic with negative antibodies but presence of HLA susceptibility
questions.exp: Latent celiac disease: asymptomatic; antibodies negative; presence of HLA susceptibility. (Book p18)

questions.q: Match the celiac spectrum label to the printed triad item — 1) Silent celiac 2) Latent celiac … A) Genetic susceptibility HLA-DQ2 or -DQ8 B) Intestinal mucosal abnormality with IgA EMA or tTG antibody positive
questions.exp: Silent celiac: intestinal mucosal abnormality with IgA EMA or tTG antibody positive; latent celiac: genetic susceptibility HLA-DQ2 or -DQ8 in a healthy individual. (Book p18)

questions.q: The pathophysiology flow chart begins with:
opts: HLA DQ2 or HLA DQ8 susceptibility
questions.exp: Pathophysiology: HLA DQ2 or HLA DQ8 susceptibility → consumption of gluten containing foods (wheat, barley, rye, oats). (Book p19)

questions.q: The gluten containing foods listed are:
questions.exp: Consumption of gluten containing foods (wheat, barley, rye, oats). (Book p19)

questions.q: The most toxic protein fraction of gluten is the:
questions.exp: Proteins → prolamine (most toxic). (Book p19)

questions.q: The chief antigen of gluten is:
questions.exp: Prolamine → gliadin (chief antigen of gluten). (Book p19)

questions.q: Gliadin with glutamine is modified by ____ in the intestinal epithelium.
questions.exp: Gliadin + glutamine → tissue transglutaminase → deamidation in the intestinal epithelium. (Book p19)

questions.q: Tissue transglutaminase acts on gliadin-bound glutamine by:
questions.exp: Tissue transglutaminase causes deamidation in the intestinal epithelium. (Book p19)

questions.q: Order the printed pathway — 1) Prolamine 2) Gliadin + glutamine 3) Tissue transglutaminase 4) Deamidated glutamine dipeptide 5) Activates T cells … A) Activates T cells B) Prolamine C) Deamidated glutamine dipeptide D) Gliadin + glutamine E) Tissue transglutaminase
questions.exp: Prolamine (most toxic) → gliadin (chief antigen) with glutamine → tissue transglutaminase → deamidated glutamine dipeptide → activates T cells → celiac disease. (Book p19)

questions.q: Polymeric IgA, which forms a dimer in this pathway, is produced from:
questions.exp: Polymeric IgA (produced from MALT) forms a dimer. (Book p19)

questions.q: Monomeric IgA is produced in the:
questions.exp: Note: monomeric IgA is produced in bone marrow. (Book p19)

questions.q: Which features are NOT seen in celiac disease, and why?
opts: Vitamin B12, magnesium and bile acid deficiency — they are reabsorbed from the distal small intestine
Steatorrhea — the distal ileum is normal
Iron deficiency anemia — iron is absorbed distally
Osteopenia — vitamin D is absorbed distally
questions.exp: Note: vitamin B12, Mg2+ and bile acid are reabsorbed from the distal small intestine → features not seen in celiac disease. (Book p19)

questions.q: On a gluten-free diet, what proportion of patients revert to normalcy?
questions.exp: Disease progression on a gluten-free diet: 90% revert to normalcy. (Book p19)

questions.q: Among the 90% who respond, clinical reversion occurs in:
questions.exp: Reverts to normalcy: clinically 3 weeks. (Book p19)

questions.q: Among the 90% who respond, histological reversion occurs in:
questions.exp: Reverts to normalcy: clinically 3 weeks, histologically 6 months. (Book p19)

questions.q: What proportion show no improvement on a gluten-free diet?
questions.exp: 10% show no improvement → refractory celiac disease. (Book p19)

questions.q: Refractory celiac disease is treated with:
questions.exp: 10% no improvement → refractory celiac disease → Rx: steroid. (Book p19)

questions.q: Classical / typical celiac disease presents with:
opts: Osmotic diarrhea, abdominal distension, foul smelling stool and weight loss
questions.exp: Classical/typical celiac: osmotic diarrhea, abdominal distension, foul smelling stool, weight loss. (Book p20)

questions.q: What proportion of celiac patients have symptoms of IBS?
questions.exp: Classical/typical celiac: symptoms of IBS (30%). (Book p20)

questions.q: Atypical celiac in children presents with:
opts: Short stature and failure to thrive
questions.exp: Atypical celiac: short stature, failure to thrive in children. (Book p20)

questions.q: Fracture and osteopenia in atypical celiac are attributed to:
questions.exp: Atypical celiac: fracture, osteopenia — ↓ vitamin D, Ca2+ absorption. (Book p20)

questions.q: Ataxia and peripheral neuropathy in atypical celiac are attributed to:
questions.exp: Atypical celiac: ataxia, peripheral neuropathy — ↓ vitamin E. (Book p20)

questions.q: Iron deficiency anemia is an atypical feature of celiac disease:
opts: If it is not due to blood loss
Only when there is overt bleeding
questions.exp: Atypical celiac: iron deficiency anemia (if not due to blood loss). (Book p20)

questions.q: Match the atypical feature to its printed mechanism — 1) Fracture, osteopenia 2) Ataxia, peripheral neuropathy 3) Iron deficiency anemia … A) Not due to blood loss B) ↓ vitamin D and Ca2+ absorption C) ↓ vitamin E
questions.exp: Fracture/osteopenia = ↓ vitamin D and Ca2+; ataxia/neuropathy = ↓ vitamin E; iron deficiency anemia = when not due to blood loss. (Book p20)

questions.q: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in celiac disease is due to:
questions.exp: Other features: secondary hyperparathyroidism — ↓ vitamin D, Ca2+. (Book p20)

questions.q: Cerebral calcifications in celiac disease are seen with:
questions.exp: Other features: calcifications in the brain seen with secondary hyperparathyroidism. (Book p20)

questions.q: Hyposplenism in celiac disease is identified by:
questions.exp: Other features: hyposplenism — presence of Howell-Jolly bodies. (Book p20)

questions.q: Follicular hyperkeratosis in celiac disease reflects deficiency of:
questions.exp: Other features: follicular hyperkeratosis — ↓ vitamin A. (Book p20)

questions.q: Edema and ascites in celiac disease reflect:
questions.exp: Other features: edema and ascites — protein malabsorption. (Book p20)

questions.q: Cryptogenic cirrhosis in celiac disease is suggested by:
questions.exp: Other features: cryptogenic cirrhosis — raised LFT. (Book p20)

questions.q: Amenorrhea, infertility and impotence are listed under:
questions.exp: Other features of celiac disease: amenorrhea, infertility, impotence. (Book p20)

questions.q: The most important definite association of celiac disease is:
questions.exp: Definite associations: dermatitis herpetiformis (most important). (Book p20)

questions.q: The skin lesions of dermatitis herpetiformis are:
opts: Papulovesicular lesions on the extensor aspect
Maculopapular lesions on the flexor aspect
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis features: papulovesicular lesions in extensor aspect. (Book p20)

questions.q: The immunofluorescence finding in dermatitis herpetiformis is:
opts: Linear IgA deposits in the dermoepidermal junction
Granular IgG deposits in the dermoepidermal junction
C3 deposits along the basement membrane
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis: linear IgA deposits in dermoepidermal junction. (Book p20)

questions.q: Cryptogenic transaminitis / cirrhosis appears in the celiac association list as a:
questions.exp: Probable associations: cryptogenic transaminitis/cirrhosis, idiopathic short stature, refractory iron deficiency anemia, cerebellar ataxia. (Book p20)

questions.q: All of the following are probable associations of celiac disease EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Probable associations: cryptogenic transaminitis/cirrhosis, idiopathic short stature, refractory iron deficiency anemia, cerebellar ataxia. Lymphocytic colitis is a definite association. (Book p20)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is a probable, not definite, association of celiac disease:
questions.exp: Probable associations: cryptogenic transaminitis/cirrhosis, idiopathic short stature, refractory iron deficiency anemia, cerebellar ataxia. The others are definite. (Book p20)

questions.q: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis in the celiac association list is also called:
questions.exp: Definite associations: hypersensitivity pneumonitis / bird-fancier lung. (Book p20)

questions.q: The serological test described as most important for diagnosis and monitoring is:
questions.exp: Serology: 1. anti-TTG antibody (IgA) — most important for diagnosis, monitoring. (Book p21)

questions.q: The specificity of anti-TTG antibody quoted in the book is:
questions.exp: Anti-TTG antibody (IgA): high sensitivity, high specificity (98%). (Book p21)

questions.q: Anti-endomysial antibody testing is performed by:
questions.exp: 2. Anti-endomysial antibody (IgA): done by indirect immunofluorescence. (Book p21)

questions.q: The sensitivity quoted for anti-endomysial antibody is:
questions.exp: Anti-endomysial antibody (IgA): high sensitivity (99%). (Book p21)

questions.q: The specificity quoted for anti-endomysial antibody is:
questions.exp: Anti-endomysial antibody (IgA): poor specificity (73%). (Book p21)

questions.q: The disadvantages listed for anti-endomysial antibody are:
questions.exp: Anti-endomysial antibody — disadvantage: subjective interpretation and cumbersome procedure. (Book p21)

questions.q: Anti-deamidated glutamine dipeptide antibody is of which isotype, and when is it used?
opts: IgG — in patients with IgA deficiency
IgA — as the first line test
questions.exp: 3. Anti-deamidated glutamine dipeptide (IgG): done in patients with IgA deficiency. (Book p21)

questions.q: The sensitivity and specificity of anti-deamidated glutamine dipeptide antibody are described as:
questions.exp: Anti-deamidated glutamine dipeptide (IgG): low sensitivity, specificity. (Book p21)

questions.q: Anti-gliadin antibody testing is described as:
questions.exp: 4. Anti-gliadin: obsolete. (Book p21)

questions.q: Match the celiac serology to its printed isotype — 1) Anti-TTG 2) Anti-endomysial 3) Anti-deamidated glutamine dipeptide … A) IgG B) IgA C) IgA
questions.exp: Anti-TTG — IgA; anti-endomysial — IgA; anti-deamidated glutamine dipeptide — IgG. (Book p21)

questions.q: The biopsy note states that the findings of celiac disease are localised to the:
questions.exp: Biopsy: 1. findings localised to mucosa. (Book p21)

questions.q: The two principal mucosal biopsy findings listed are:
opts: Total villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia
questions.exp: Biopsy: 2. total villous atrophy, 3. crypt hyperplasia. (Book p21)

questions.q: Mucosal thickness in celiac biopsy is:
questions.exp: Biopsy: 4. normal mucosal thickness. (Book p21)

questions.q: Lymphocyte infiltrates in celiac biopsy are seen in the:
questions.exp: Biopsy: 5. lymphocyte infiltrates in lamina propria. (Book p21)

questions.q: The biopsy finding described as non-specific is:
questions.exp: Biopsy: 6. vascular degeneration of surface epithelium (non-specific). (Book p21)

questions.q: The grading system shown next to the celiac biopsy image is the ____ score.
questions.exp: Biopsy image: celiac disease during reversibility with the Marsh score. (Book p21)

questions.q: Interpret the serology and biopsy combinations as printed — 1) Both positive 2) Both negative 3) Serology positive, biopsy negative 4) Serology negative, biopsy positive … A) Repeat biopsy B) Celiac disease C) Not celiac disease; biopsy findings non-specific D) Not celiac disease; if features suggestive, test HLA DQ2/DQ8
questions.exp: Both +ve → celiac disease; both −ve → not celiac disease (if features suggestive → HLA DQ2/DQ8); serology +ve/biopsy −ve → repeat biopsy; serology −ve/biopsy +ve → not celiac disease, biopsy findings non-specific. (Book p22)

questions.q: When both serology and biopsy are negative but features still suggest celiac disease, the book advises:
questions.exp: Both −ve → not celiac disease; if features suggestive of celiac disease → HLA DQ2/DQ8. (Book p22)

questions.q: Serology negative but biopsy positive is interpreted as:
opts: Not celiac disease — the biopsy findings are non-specific
questions.exp: Serology −ve, biopsy +ve → not celiac disease; biopsy findings are non-specific. (Book p22)

questions.q: The examples given of non-specific biopsy findings with negative serology are:
opts: Tropical sprue and cow's milk intolerance
questions.exp: Non-specific biopsy findings e.g.: tropical sprue, cow's milk intolerance. (Book p22)

questions.q: Complications of celiac disease are seen in:
questions.exp: Complications: seen in refractory celiac disease. (Book p22)

questions.q: The most common malignancy complicating celiac disease is:
questions.exp: It is a premalignant condition: enteropathy associated T-cell lymphoma (m/c). (Book p22)

questions.q: Besides lymphoma, the premalignant complications listed are:
opts: Small intestinal adenocarcinoma and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
questions.exp: Premalignant: enteropathy associated T-cell lymphoma (m/c), small intestinal adenocarcinoma, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. (Book p22)

questions.q: The diet advised in celiac treatment is based on:
opts: Rice, corn, maize, potato and soybean
questions.exp: Treatment — diet: rice, corn, maize, potato, soybean based. (Book p22)

questions.q: The dietary restriction in celiac disease is of:
questions.exp: Treatment — diet: restriction of wheat, barley, rye, oats. (Book p22)

questions.q: A patient with biopsy-proven celiac disease has persistent villous atrophy after 12 months of strict gluten withdrawal. The book's next step is:
questions.exp: 10% show no improvement → refractory celiac disease → Rx: steroid. (Book p22)

questions.q: Whipple's disease is described as:
opts: Chronic multisystem involvement of joints, GIT, CNS and CVS
A disease of the biliary tree
questions.exp: Whipple's disease — presentation: chronic multisystem involvement (joints, GIT, CNS, CVS). (Book p22)

questions.q: The demographic described for Whipple's disease is:
questions.exp: Presentation: M > F, 50-60 yrs. (Book p22)

questions.q: The intestinal involvement in Whipple's disease is:
questions.exp: Presentation: pan-intestinal — proximal > distal. (Book p22)

questions.q: The organism causing Whipple's disease is:
opts: Tropheryma whipplei — a gram positive actinobacterium
questions.exp: Tropheryma whipplei: gram +ve actinobacterium. (Book p22)

questions.q: Tropheryma whipplei cannot be cultured because of its:
opts: Inability to grow on any known medium
questions.exp: Tropheryma whipplei: gram +ve actinobacterium that cannot be cultured d/t slow doubling time. (Book p22)

questions.q: Diagnosis of Whipple's disease is by:
questions.exp: Whipple's disease — Dx: biopsy. (Book p22)

questions.q: Joint symptoms are the first symptom in what proportion of Whipple's disease?
questions.exp: Joints: first symptom in >80% cases. (Book p23)

questions.q: The joints predominantly involved in Whipple's disease are:
questions.exp: Joints: predominance — large joints (knee). (Book p23)

questions.q: The joint pattern in Whipple's disease is:
questions.exp: Joints: pattern — migratory arthralgia > arthritis. (Book p23)

questions.q: Gastrointestinal features appear:
questions.exp: GIT: 2-3 yrs after joint features. (Book p23)

questions.q: The most consistent gastrointestinal feature of Whipple's disease is:
questions.exp: GIT: diarrhea (most consistent). (Book p23)

questions.q: Besides diarrhea and weight loss, the GIT column lists:
questions.exp: GIT: diarrhea (most consistent), weight loss, abdominal pain + mesenteric lymphadenopathy. (Book p23)

questions.q: Neurological involvement occurs in what proportion of Whipple's disease?
questions.exp: Neuro Whipple's (40%). (Book p23)

questions.q: The most common neurological manifestation of Whipple's disease is:
questions.exp: Neuro Whipple's: m/c neurological manifestation — rapidly progressive dementia. (Book p23)

questions.q: The most specific neurological manifestation of Whipple's disease is:
questions.exp: Neuro Whipple's: m/c specific manifestation — oculomasticatory myorhythmia > oculofacial myorhythmia. (Book p23)

questions.q: Oculomasticatory myorhythmia consists of:
questions.exp: Oculomasticatory myorhythmia: pendular nystagmus + masticatory arrhythmias. (Book p23)

questions.q: Oculomasticatory myorhythmia is associated with:
questions.exp: Oculomasticatory myorhythmia is associated with supranuclear ophthalmoplegia. (Book p23)

questions.q: Relapse with CNS manifestations in Whipple's disease indicates:
questions.exp: Relapse associated with CNS manifestations: bad prognosis. (Book p23)

questions.q: The CVS lesion of Whipple's disease is:
opts: Culture negative endocarditis, mitral valve more than myocarditis more than pericarditis
questions.exp: CVS: culture negative endocarditis — mitral valve > myocarditis > pericarditis. (Book p23)

questions.q: Culture negative endocarditis in Whipple's disease is caused by which group?
questions.exp: Culture negative endocarditis: HACEK group. (Book p23)

questions.q: Match the HACEK organisms as printed — 1) H 2) A 3) C 4) E 5) K … A) Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans B) Haemophilus C) Kingella D) Cardiobacter E) Eikenella
questions.exp: HACEK: Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacter, Eikenella, Kingella. (Book p23)

questions.q: The tetrad illustrated for Whipple's disease consists of:
opts: Joint symptoms, diarrhea, weight loss, and abdominal pain with mesenteric lymphadenopathy
questions.exp: Whipple's tetrad: joint symptoms, diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal pain + mesenteric lymphadenopathy. (Book p23)

questions.q: Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is described as diagnostic in what proportion?
questions.exp: Diagnosis: upper GI endoscopy — biopsy: 100%. (Book p23)

questions.q: The PCR test in Whipple's disease identifies:
questions.exp: Diagnosis: PCR — identification of Tropheryma whipplei. (Book p23)

questions.q: Match the differential of Whipple's disease to the system — 1) Joint symptoms 2) GIT symptoms … A) TB B) Spondyloarthritis
questions.exp: Differential diagnosis: joint symptoms — spondyloarthritis; GIT symptoms — TB. (Book p23)

questions.q: The best induction regimen for Whipple's disease is:
questions.exp: Treatment — induction: IV ceftriaxone 2 g × 14 days: best regimen. (Book p24)

questions.q: Alternatives listed for induction in Whipple's disease are:
questions.exp: Induction: IV ceftriaxone 2 g × 14 days (best), meropenem, penicillin + streptomycin. (Book p24)

questions.q: Maintenance therapy in Whipple's disease is with:
questions.exp: Maintenance: co-trimoxazole (DOC). (Book p24)

questions.q: The stated advantages of co-trimoxazole maintenance are:
opts: Prevents relapse and has good CNS penetration
Sterilises the gut and corrects folate deficiency
questions.exp: Maintenance: co-trimoxazole — prevent relapse, good CNS penetration. (Book p24)

questions.q: The diagnostic biopsy in Whipple's disease shows:
opts: PAS positive foamy macrophages in epithelium, lamina propria and submucosa
Total villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia
questions.exp: Biopsy: PAS +ve foamy macrophages seen in epithelium, lamina propria, submucosa; macrophages contain the organism. (Book p24)

questions.q: The villi in the Whipple's biopsy image are described as:
questions.exp: Biopsy image: PAS +ve foamy macrophages with enlarged villi. (Book p24)

questions.q: Tropical sprue is the most common cause of malabsorption in:
questions.exp: Tropical sprue: m/c cause of malabsorption in India, Bangladesh, Pakistan. (Book p24)

questions.q: Histologically, tropical sprue resembles:
questions.exp: Tropical sprue: histological features similar to celiac disease. (Book p24)

questions.q: The initiating event in the printed pathogenesis of tropical sprue is:
questions.exp: Pathogenesis: infective diarrhea → presence of toxigenic coliform in intestine. (Book p24)

questions.q: The toxigenic coliforms implicated in tropical sprue are:
questions.exp: Presence of toxigenic coliform in intestine (E. coli, Klebsiella). (Book p24)

questions.q: The major fermentation product implicated in tropical sprue is:
questions.exp: Fermentation products (major product: ethanol). (Book p24)

questions.q: Structural damage to the small intestine in tropical sprue impairs absorption of:
questions.exp: Structural damage to small intestine → impairs absorption of folic acid. (Book p24)

questions.q: The interval after which pan-intestinal involvement develops is:
questions.exp: Impaired folic acid absorption → 2-3 weeks → pan-intestinal involvement. (Book p24)

questions.q: Pan-intestinal involvement causes defective absorption of:
opts: Vitamin B12, bile acid and Mg2+
questions.exp: Pan-intestinal involvement → defective B12, bile acid, Mg2+ absorption. (Book p24)

questions.q: The diarrhea of tropical sprue is described as:
opts: Chronic small bowel diarrhea that is watery and voluminous
Large bowel diarrhea with blood and mucus
Factitious diarrhea with normal stool osmolality
questions.exp: Clinical features: chronic small bowel diarrhea (watery, voluminous). (Book p25)

questions.q: The most prominent deficiency in tropical sprue is:
questions.exp: Clinical features: folic acid deficiency (most prominent). (Book p25)

questions.q: Hyperpigmentation in tropical sprue is attributed to:
questions.exp: Clinical features: hyperpigmentation — d/t B12 deficiency. (Book p25)

questions.q: Biopsy in tropical sprue shows:
questions.exp: Investigations: biopsy — features of celiac disease. (Book p25)

questions.q: Serology in tropical sprue is:
questions.exp: Investigations: serology — negative. (Book p25)

questions.q: Stool examination in tropical sprue is performed for:
opts: Ova, cyst and trophozoite to rule out giardiasis
questions.exp: Investigations: stool examination for ova, cyst, trophozoite (to rule out giardiasis). (Book p25)

questions.q: The treatment of tropical sprue is:
opts: Folic acid 5 mg daily plus tetracycline 250 mg QID for 3-6 months
questions.exp: Treatment: folic acid 5 mg daily + tetracycline 250 mg QID for 3-6 months. (Book p25)

questions.q: The dose of folic acid used in tropical sprue is:
questions.exp: Treatment: folic acid 5 mg daily. (Book p25)

questions.q: The dose and frequency of tetracycline used in tropical sprue is:
questions.exp: Treatment: tetracycline 250 mg QID. (Book p25)

questions.q: The duration of tropical sprue treatment is:
questions.exp: Treatment: folic acid + tetracycline for 3-6 months. (Book p25)

questions.q: Relapse occurs in what proportion of treated tropical sprue?
questions.exp: Note: relapse in 20% of cases. (Book p25)

questions.q: In SIBO the organism uses vitamin B12 and therefore:
questions.exp: Note: in SIBO the organism uses B12 → synthesises folic acid. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: Bile acid diarrhea is also known as:
questions.exp: Bile acid diarrhea: AKA cholorrhea. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: Bile acid diarrhea is seen in:
questions.exp: Bile acid diarrhea: seen in tropical sprue. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: Bile acid diarrhea is due to defective:
questions.exp: Bile acid diarrhea: due to defective FGF-19. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: Defective FGF-19 leads to:
opts: ↓ bile acid released in the ileum
↑ bile acid synthesis in the colon
questions.exp: Pathology: defective FGF-19 → ↓ bile acid released in the ileum. (Book p25)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: In limited ileal disease, FGF-19 is present in limited quantity so the liver:
opts: Produces excess bile acid as compensation
questions.exp: Limited ileal disease: FGF-19 +ve in limited quantity → liver produces excess bile acid (compensatory). (Book p26)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: In bile acid diarrhea, bile acid in the intestinal lumen removes:
opts: Na+, Cl− and K+ from the intestinal epithelium
Calcium and oxalate from the lumen
questions.exp: Bile acid removes Na+, Cl−, K+ from intestinal epithelium → bile acid diarrhea. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: The statement made about bile acid diarrhea is that there is:
questions.exp: Bile acid diarrhea: no steatorrhea / malabsorption. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: Fatty acid diarrhea occurs with:
questions.exp: Fatty acid diarrhea: severe ileal disease. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: Order the printed fatty acid diarrhea pathway — 1) Severe ileal disease 2) Impaired reabsorption of bile acid 3) No compensatory release 4) Malabsorption 5) Fatty acid in colon … A) Malabsorption B) Severe ileal disease C) Fatty acid in colon D) No compensatory release E) Impaired reabsorption of bile acid
questions.exp: Severe ileal disease → impaired reabsorption of bile acid → no compensatory release → malabsorption → fatty acid in colon. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: The steatorrhea of fatty acid diarrhea is quantified in the book as:
questions.exp: Fatty acid diarrhea: fatty acid in colon → steatorrhea (> 20 g). (Book p26)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: Match the treatment response as printed — 1) Bile acid diarrhea 2) Fatty acid diarrhea … A) Responds to low-fat diet B) Responds to cholestyramine
questions.exp: Response to cholestyramine: yes in bile acid diarrhea, no in fatty acid diarrhea; response to low-fat diet: no in bile acid diarrhea, yes in fatty acid diarrhea. (Book p26)

questions.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
questions.q: A patient with ileal disease has watery diarrhea without steatorrhea. Cholestyramine abolishes the diarrhea. This fits:
questions.exp: Bile acid diarrhea: no steatorrhea and responds to cholestyramine. (Book p26)

questions.q: Short bowel syndrome is defined as a small intestinal length below:
questions.exp: Length of small intestine: short bowel syndrome < 200 cm. (Book p26)

questions.q: Very severe short bowel syndrome is defined as a length below:

questions.exp: Unabsorbed long chain fatty acids → free oxalate → into blood → oxalate stones in urine. (Book p27)

questions.q: Cholesterol gallstones in short bowel syndrome are attributed to:

questions.exp: Bacterial overgrowth (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium) → D-lactate (not metabolised). (Book p27)

questions.exp: D-lactate (not metabolised) → absorbed into blood → D-lactic acidosis → CNS manifestations. (Book p27)

questions.q: Hypergastrinemia in short bowel syndrome arises because:
opts: Absent small bowel reduces intestinal hormones, leaving gastrin uninhibited
questions.exp: Hypergastrinemia: absent small bowel → ↓ intestinal hormones → gastrin uninhibited. (Book p27)

questions.q: Hypomagnesemia in short bowel syndrome is due to:

questions.exp: Hypomagnesemia: no Mg2+ absorption from ileum. (Book p27)

questions.exp: Physiology: GLP-1, GLP-2, peptide YY → ↓ motility → ↓ gastric emptying (ileal break). (Book p27)

questions.q: The ileal break is triggered when unabsorbed ____ enters the ileum.
questions.exp: Ileal break: ↑ unabsorbed fat enters ileum. (Book p27)

questions.q: Calcium, folate and vitamins A, D and E deficiency occur with absence of the:
questions.exp: Deficiencies: Ca2+, folate, vitamin A, D, E — in absent jejunum. (Book p28)

It is absorbed in the stomach
It is given routinely in parenteral nutrition

questions.q: SIBO in short bowel syndrome is attributed to:

They are the most energy dense

Absorbed without digestion in the duodenum

The only source of essential fatty acids

questions.q: When the colon is absent, the management column advises:

questions.q: The medical therapy listed for short bowel syndrome is:

questions.q: SIBO is also known as:

questions.exp: SIBO: AKA blind loop syndrome, stagnant bowel syndrome. (Book p28)

questions.q: Match the region to its printed normal bacterial content — 1) Proximal small intestine 2) Ileum 3) Colon … A) Anaerobes B) No bacteria C) Enterobacteriaceae
questions.exp: Physiology: proximal small intestine — no bacteria; ileum — Enterobacteriaceae; colon — anaerobes. (Book p28)

questions.q: The organisms causing bacterial overgrowth in SIBO are:
opts: Non-toxigenic anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis, Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas
Toxigenic aerobes such as E. coli and Klebsiella
questions.exp: Pathology: non-toxigenic anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas). (Book p28)

questions.q: In SIBO the overgrowth occurs in the:
questions.exp: Pathology: bacterial overgrowth in the proximal small intestine. (Book p28)

questions.q: The anatomical defects listed as causes of SIBO are:

IBS, achalasia, gastroparesis and Hirschsprung disease
Diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism and Addison disease

questions.exp: 4. Immunodeficiency: common variable immune deficiency (CVID), IgA deficiency. (Book p29)

questions.q: The most common symptom of SIBO is:
questions.exp: Bloating, belching: m/c symptom. (Book p29)

units.title: Global Malabsorption: Overview
units.guide:
Defective absorption of carbohydrate, fat and protein from small intestinal mucosal dysfunction.
Fat is the most sensitive, most specific and most energy dense nutrient.
Three causes: celiac disease, Whipple's disease, tropical sprue.

units.title: Celiac Disease: Features & Iceberg Phenomenon
units.guide:
AKA celiac sprue / gluten sensitive enteropathy / non-tropical sprue.
Iceberg phenomenon: only 50% present classically, missed through physician unawareness.
HLA DQ2/DQ8 is the most important predisposition; the disease is proximal small intestinal.

units.title: Celiac Disease: Types
units.guide:
Classical: 50% present with symptoms of malabsorption.
Atypical: symptoms other than malabsorption; silent: asymptomatic, serology positive.
Latent: asymptomatic, antibodies negative, HLA susceptibility present.

units.title: Celiac Pathophysiology & Disease Progression
units.guide:
HLA DQ2/DQ8 → gluten (wheat, barley, rye, oats) → prolamine (most toxic) → gliadin (chief antigen).
Tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin-bound glutamine → activates T cells.
Gluten-free diet: 90% revert (clinically 3 weeks, histologically 6 months); 10% refractory → steroids.

units.title: Celiac Clinical Features
units.guide:
Classical: osmotic diarrhea, distension, foul smelling stool, weight loss; IBS symptoms in 30%.
Atypical: short stature, fracture/osteopenia, ataxia/neuropathy, iron deficiency anemia not due to blood loss.
Other: secondary hyperparathyroidism, cerebral calcification, hyposplenism with Howell-Jolly bodies, follicular hyperkeratosis, edema/ascites, cryptogenic cirrhosis.

units.title: Celiac Associations
units.guide:
Definite: dermatitis herpetiformis (most important), Down syndrome, type I DM, IgA nephropathy, IgA deficiency, bird-fancier lung, lymphocytic colitis, cerebral calcification with epilepsy.
Dermatitis herpetiformis: papulovesicular extensor lesions with linear IgA at the dermoepidermal junction.
Probable: cryptogenic transaminitis, idiopathic short stature, refractory iron deficiency anemia, cerebellar ataxia.

units.title: Celiac Diagnosis: Serology & Biopsy
units.guide:
Anti-TTG IgA: most important for diagnosis and monitoring; specificity 98%.
Anti-endomysial IgA: indirect immunofluorescence, sensitivity 99%, specificity 73%, subjective and cumbersome.
Anti-deamidated gliadin peptide IgG for IgA deficiency; anti-gliadin obsolete. Biopsy: mucosal total villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, normal thickness, lamina propria lymphocytes, Marsh score.

units.title: Celiac Interpretation, Complications & Treatment
units.guide:
Both positive = celiac; both negative = not celiac (test HLA DQ2/DQ8 if suggestive).
Serology positive/biopsy negative: repeat biopsy; serology negative/biopsy positive: non-specific (tropical sprue, cow's milk intolerance).
Refractory disease is premalignant: EATL, small intestinal adenocarcinoma, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma; diet is rice/corn/maize/potato/soybean with gluten restriction.

units.title: Whipple's Disease: Presentation
units.guide:
Chronic multisystem disease of joints, GIT, CNS and CVS; M > F, 50-60 years.
Pan-intestinal, proximal more than distal; Tropheryma whipplei is a gram positive actinobacterium that cannot be cultured because of slow doubling time.
Diagnosis is by biopsy.

units.title: Whipple's Disease: Clinical Features
units.guide:
Joints first in >80%: large joints, migratory arthralgia > arthritis.
GIT 2-3 years later: diarrhea (most consistent), weight loss, abdominal pain with mesenteric lymphadenopathy.
Neuro 40%: rapidly progressive dementia (m/c) and oculomasticatory myorhythmia (m/c specific); CVS: culture negative endocarditis, mitral valve > myocarditis > pericarditis, HACEK group.

units.title: Whipple's Disease: Diagnosis & Treatment
units.guide:
Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy is 100% diagnostic; PCR identifies Tropheryma whipplei.
PAS positive foamy macrophages in epithelium, lamina propria and submucosa with enlarged villi.
Induction IV ceftriaxone 2 g for 14 days (best); maintenance co-trimoxazole prevents relapse and penetrates the CNS.

units.title: Tropical Sprue: Pathogenesis
units.guide:
Most common cause of malabsorption in India, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Infective diarrhea → toxigenic coliforms (E. coli, Klebsiella) → fermentation products, mainly ethanol.
Structural damage impairs folic acid absorption → 2-3 weeks → pan-intestinal involvement with defective B12, bile acid and Mg2+ absorption.

units.title: Tropical Sprue: Features, Investigations & Treatment
units.guide:
Chronic watery voluminous small bowel diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, prominent folic acid deficiency, hyperpigmentation from B12 deficiency.
Biopsy resembles celiac disease but serology is negative; stool examined for ova, cyst and trophozoite to rule out giardiasis.
Folic acid 5 mg daily plus tetracycline 250 mg QID for 3-6 months; relapse in 20%.

units.title: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
units.sec: Bile Acid Diarrhea & Fatty Acid Diarrhea
units.guide:
Bile acid diarrhea (cholorrhea) is seen in tropical sprue from defective FGF-19; limited ileal disease leaves compensatory excess hepatic bile acid removing Na+, Cl− and K+.
Fatty acid diarrhea needs severe ileal disease: no compensatory release → malabsorption → fatty acid in colon → steatorrhea >20 g.
Cholestyramine helps bile acid diarrhea; a low-fat diet helps fatty acid diarrhea.

units.title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Definition & Etiology
units.guide:
Short bowel syndrome: < 200 cm; very severe: < 100 cm.
Adult: mesenteric vascular disease (ischemia with resection) more than Crohn's disease.
Child: necrotising enterocolitis.

units.title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Clinical Presentation
units.guide:
Hyperoxaluria: unabsorbed LCFA bind calcium, free oxalate is absorbed and forms oxalate stones.
Absent ileum → cholesterol gallstones from supersaturation.
D-lactic acidosis from gram positive anaerobes (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium) causing CNS features; hypergastrinemia; hypomagnesemia; defective ileal break with rapid gastric emptying.

units.title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Deficiencies & Management
units.guide:
Iron: absent duodenum > jejunum; Ca2+, folate, vitamins A, D, E: absent jejunum; vitamin K rarely because bacteria migrate when the ileocecal valve is lost.
SIBO from loss of the ileocecal valve.
Diet: medium chain fatty acids and complex carbohydrates; total parenteral nutrition when the colon is absent; teduglutide is an oral GLP-2 analogue.

units.title: SIBO: Physiology, Pathology & Etiology
units.guide:
AKA blind loop syndrome / stagnant bowel syndrome.
Proximal small intestine normally has no bacteria; ileum has Enterobacteriaceae; colon has anaerobes.
Overgrowth of non-toxigenic anaerobes proximally; causes are anatomical defects, motility disorders (IBS, scleroderma, diabetes, amyloidosis), immunodeficiency and HIV.

units.title: SIBO: Presentation, Investigations & Management
units.guide:
Bacteria compete for nutrients and consume B12: bloating and belching are most common; B12 deficiency, macrocytic anemia, steatorrhea, unexplained diarrhea.
Jejunal aspirate >10^3 CFU/mL is gold standard; lactulose H2 breath test is preferred; indican is obsolete; B12 low, folate and vitamin K high.
Rifaximin 550 mg BD for 7-10 days; avoid macrolides.
